If either run fails, I will show you the output and stop. I will not report the change as done.

**Why the scope is small**
- No other code reads `DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE`. Only this one constant changes.
- `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` stays at 500. The new default is well under that cap, so no request that is valid today becomes invalid.
- Clients that send an explicit page size see no change. Only callers that omit it get 100 rows instead of 50.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The code risk here is close to zero. The real risk is in the behavior that callers see. A client that omits the page size now gets responses about twice as large. A client that assumes 50 rows per page can also break, for example when it computes a page count or an offset.
- The fact that nothing else reads the constant tells you about the server only. Docs, an OpenAPI spec or a frontend can still state "50" as a literal value. That is why I searched for literal values as well as for the constant name.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
